GENETIC INFORMATION NONDISCRIMINATION ACT (GINA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008 (GINA), a federal employment-discrimination statute, as it relates to Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee. It states facts about what GINA prohibits with respect to genetic information in employment, the specific statutory exceptions that let an employer request or acquire genetic information in limited circumstances, and the confidentiality requirement that applies to genetic information an employer lawfully holds. Genetic information is a category of information distinct from the disability-related medical information addressed by the Americans with Disabilities Act; this document does not restate ADA obligations and is not itself a medical inquiry, a consent form, or an authorization for any specific request. It does not tell Acme, Inc. or Jordan Lee whether any particular request, inquiry, or record involves genetic information under GINA, or what to do about any specific situation.

DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF GENETIC INFORMATION IS AN UNLAWFUL EMPLOYMENT PRACTICE
Federal law makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to fail or refuse to hire, to discharge, or otherwise to discriminate against an employee with respect to compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of genetic information with respect to that employee. It is separately an unlawful employment practice for an employer to limit, segregate, or classify its employees in a way that would deprive or tend to deprive an employee of employment opportunities, or that would otherwise adversely affect the employee's status as an employee, because of genetic information with respect to that employee. Under the statute's own definitions, this protection extends to applicants as well as current employees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer — (1) to fail or refuse to hire, or to discharge, any employee , or otherwise to discriminate against any employee with respect to the compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment of the employee , because of genetic information with respect to the employee; or (2) to limit, segregate, or classify the employees of the employer in any way that would deprive or tend to deprive any employee of employment opportunities or otherwise adversely affect the status of the employee as an employee, because of genetic information with respect to the employee."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-1(a) (Cornell LII text), Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, Title II, employer practices — discrimination based on genetic information (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000ff-1)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory subsection, 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-1(a), quoted in full below; it is not corroborated by a second, independent statutory source. The point that the statute's protection extends to applicants comes from GINA's own definitions section, 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff(2)(A)(i), which defines 'employee' by cross-reference to a Title VII definition that itself includes an applicant; that cross-reference was reviewed in this research but is not separately quoted as a citation here, and is stated in the body as a summarized fact rather than a directly verified quote. This clause states only that the described conduct is an unlawful employment practice under the statute; it does not determine whether any specific employer's treatment of any specific individual was because of genetic information, and it does not address the separate, narrower restriction on requesting or acquiring genetic information in the first place, which is covered in a later clause.

WHAT COUNTS AS "GENETIC INFORMATION" UNDER GINA
GINA defines "genetic information," with respect to an individual, as information about: the individual's own genetic tests; the genetic tests of the individual's family members; and the manifestation of a disease or disorder in the individual's family members. This third category is commonly described as family medical history, and the statute's definition reaches it directly — GINA's protection is not limited to genetic tests alone. The definition also includes, for any individual, a request for or receipt of genetic services, or participation in clinical research that includes genetic services, by that individual or a family member. The statute separately defines "genetic test" as an analysis of human DNA, RNA, chromosomes, proteins, or metabolites that detects genotypes, mutations, or chromosomal changes, and it expressly excludes an analysis of proteins or metabolites that does not detect genotypes, mutations, or chromosomal changes. The definition of "genetic information" expressly excludes information about an individual's sex or age.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The term “ genetic information ” means, with respect to any individual, information about— (i) such individual’s genetic tests , (ii) the genetic tests of family members of such individual, and (iii) the manifestation of a disease or disorder in family members of such individual. (B) Inclusion of genetic services and participation in genetic research Such term includes, with respect to any individual, any request for, or receipt of, genetic services , or participation in clinical research which includes genetic services , by such individual or any family member of such individual. (C) Exclusions The term “ genetic information ” shall not include information about the sex or age of any individual."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff(4) (Cornell LII text), GINA, Title II, definitions — "genetic information" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000ff)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory section, 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff(4) (with the 'genetic test' definition drawn from paragraph (7) of that same section); these paragraphs are subsections of one section and are not independent sources of one another. The statute's definition of 'family member' (42 U.S.C. § 2000ff(3)) — which reaches first-, second-, third-, and fourth-degree relatives of the individual, plus certain dependents — was reviewed as part of this research but is not separately quoted or made a citation in this clause; a reader should not assume 'family member' is limited to immediate family for GINA purposes. This clause states the statutory definition only; it does not determine whether any particular piece of information about any specific individual meets that definition.

RESTRICTION ON REQUESTING, REQUIRING, OR PURCHASING GENETIC INFORMATION
Separately from the discrimination prohibition described above, federal law makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to request, require, or purchase genetic information with respect to an employee or a family member of the employee, subject to six specific statutory exceptions. Those exceptions apply where: (1) the employer inadvertently requests or requires family medical history; (2) the employer offers health or genetic services, including as part of a wellness program, the employee has given prior, knowing, voluntary, written authorization, and specific statutory limits are met on who may receive individually identifiable results and how the employer may receive them; (3) the employer requests or requires family medical history from the employee to comply with the certification provisions of the federal Family and Medical Leave Act or a comparable state family and medical leave law; (4) the employer purchases documents that are commercially and publicly available — such as newspapers, magazines, periodicals, and books, but not including medical databases or court records — that happen to include family medical history; (5) the information is used for genetic monitoring of the biological effects of toxic substances in the workplace, subject to written-notice, authorization-or-legal-mandate, individual-results, regulatory-compliance, and aggregate-reporting conditions specified in the statute; or (6) the employer conducts DNA analysis for law enforcement purposes as a forensic laboratory or for human remains identification, limited to using the results for quality-control analysis of DNA identification markers to detect sample contamination.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to request, require, or purchase genetic information with respect to an employee or a family member of the employee except— (1) where an employer inadvertently requests or requires family medical history of the employee or family member of the employee; (2) where— (A) health or genetic services are offered by the employer, including such services offered as part of a wellness program; (B) the employee provides prior, knowing, voluntary, and written authorization; (C) only the employee (or family member if the family member is receiving genetic services ) and the licensed health care professional or board certified genetic counselor involved in providing such services receive individually identifiable information concerning the results of such services; and (D) any individually identifiable genetic information provided under subparagraph (C) in connection with the services provided under subparagraph (A) is only available for purposes of such services and shall not be disclosed to the employer except in aggregate terms that do not disclose the identity of specific employees; (3) where an employer requests or requires family medical history from the employee to comply with the certification provisions of section 2613 of title 29 or such requirements under State family and medical leave laws; (4) where an employer purchases documents that are commercially and publicly available (including newspapers, magazines, periodicals, and books, but not including medical databases or court records) that include family medical history; (5) where the information involved is to be used for genetic monitoring of the biological effects of toxic substances in the workplace, but only if— (A) the employer provides written notice of the genetic monitoring to the employee; (B) (i) the employee provides prior, knowing, voluntary, and written authorization; or (ii) the genetic monitoring is required by Federal or State law; (C) the employee is informed of individual monitoring results; (D) the monitoring is in compliance with— (i) any Federal genetic monitoring regulations, including any such regulations that may be promulgated by the Secretary of Labor pursuant to the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 ( 29 U.S.C. 651 et seq.), the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 ( 30 U.S.C. 801 et seq.), or the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 ( 42 U.S.C. 2011 et seq.); or (ii) State genetic monitoring regulations, in the case of a State that is implementing genetic monitoring regulations under the authority of the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 ( 29 U.S.C. 651 et seq.); and (E) the employer , excluding any licensed health care professional or board certified genetic counselor that is involved in the genetic monitoring program, receives the results of the monitoring only in aggregate terms that do not disclose the identity of specific employees; or (6) where the employer conducts DNA analysis for law enforcement purposes as a forensic laboratory or for purposes of human remains identification, and requests or requires genetic information of such employer’ s employees, but only to the extent that such genetic information is used for analysis of DNA identification markers for quality control to detect sample contamination."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-1(b) (Cornell LII text), GINA, Title II, employer practices — acquisition of genetic information and statutory exceptions (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000ff-1)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory subsection, 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-1(b), quoted here in full; it is not corroborated by a second, independent source. Each of the six exceptions carries additional statutory conditions beyond the short description in this clause's body — for example, the genetic-monitoring exception (5) has five separate lettered sub-conditions, and the wellness-program exception (2) has four lettered sub-conditions — all of which appear in the quoted text below but are only summarized, not individually restated, in the body above. This clause does not determine whether any specific employer's request, requirement, or purchase of information about any specific individual falls within or outside any of these exceptions.

CONFIDENTIALITY OF GENETIC INFORMATION THE EMPLOYER LAWFULLY HOLDS
If an employer possesses genetic information about an employee, federal law requires that information to be maintained on separate forms and in separate medical files, and treated as a confidential medical record of the employee. The statute itself provides a specific route to compliance: an employer is considered to be in compliance with this requirement if the genetic information is maintained with, and treated as, a confidential medical record under the Americans with Disabilities Act's own post-offer medical-examination confidentiality provision, 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(3)(B). Federal law also limits disclosure of genetic information the employer holds to a specific, enumerated list of circumstances, including disclosure to the employee at the employee's own written request, in response to a court order (limited to the information the order expressly authorizes), to government officials investigating compliance, in connection with an employee's compliance with family-and-medical-leave certification requirements, and to certain researchers and public health agencies under conditions specified in the statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If an employer , employment agency , labor organization , or joint labor-management committee possesses genetic information about an employee or member, such information shall be maintained on separate forms and in separate medical files and be treated as a confidential medical record of the employee or member. An employer, employment agency, labor organization, or joint labor-management committee shall be considered to be in compliance with the maintenance of information requirements of this subsection with respect to genetic information subject to this subsection that is maintained with and treated as a confidential medical record under section 12112(d)(3)(B) of this title ."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-5(a) (Cornell LII text), GINA, Title II — confidentiality of genetic information, treatment as part of confidential medical record (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000ff-5)
  Known gap: The confidentiality requirement (42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-5(a)) and the disclosure-limitation list (42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-5(b)) are both part of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another; they are treated here as one connected source, and the disclosure-limitation list is summarized rather than separately quoted. The statute's own text ties GINA confidentiality directly to the ADA's confidentiality provision, 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(3)(B) — it states that an employer maintaining genetic information in compliance with that ADA provision is considered to be in compliance with GINA's own separate-forms/separate-files requirement — but that ADA provision's text was not independently re-fetched and re-verified in this research session; the fact that GINA cross-references it is verified below, but the ADA text itself is not separately confirmed here. A reader should not assume the two confidentiality regimes are identical in every respect, only that the statute makes compliance with one a recognized route to compliance with the other. This clause does not itemize every sub-condition of the disclosure exceptions listed in the statute, and it does not determine whether any specific disclosure by any specific employer is permitted.

WHICH EMPLOYERS ARE COVERED: THE FIFTEEN-EMPLOYEE THRESHOLD
GINA's employment provisions apply only to an "employer" as the statute defines that term. GINA's own definitions section defines "employer" for the ordinary private-sector case by cross-reference to the definition used in Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b) (GINA's definitions section also cross-references several narrower categories covering certain federal, state, and congressional employers, not addressed here). Title VII's definition, which GINA borrows in this way, defines "employer" as a person engaged in an industry affecting commerce who has fifteen or more employees for each working day in each of twenty or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year, subject to specific statutory exclusions, including the United States, corporations wholly owned by the United States government, Indian tribes, and certain bona fide private membership clubs exempt from taxation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The term “ employer ” means— (i) an employer (as defined in section 2000e(b) of this title );"
  — 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff(2)(B)(i) (Cornell LII text), GINA, Title II, definitions — "employer," cross-reference to Title VII definition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000ff)
  "The term “ employer ” means a person engaged in an industry affecting commerce who has fifteen or more employees for each working day in each of twenty or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year"
  — 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b) (Cornell LII text), Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title VII, definitions — "employer," fifteen-or-more-employees threshold (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000e)
  Known gap: These two citations are not independent corroboration of the same point: 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff(2)(B)(i) is GINA's own definitions section, and it establishes the fifteen-employee threshold only by cross-referencing 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b), a separate section of Title VII that GINA's text incorporates rather than restates; the two are genuinely distinct, independently numbered sections of the U.S. Code, but one supplies the actual numeric threshold that the other merely borrows by reference, so they are presented together as a citation chain rather than as two independent sources reaching the same conclusion. This clause does not address the several other, narrower employer categories GINA's definition also cross-references (state employees, congressional employees, and certain other federal employees under Title 2 and Title 3 of the U.S. Code), and it does not determine whether any specific entity meets the fifteen-or-more-employees threshold in any given year.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate that you have received and reviewed this information sheet.

Applicant / Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________
